ABSTRACT
This paper presents a comprehensive long-term stochastic mixed-integer single-level single-stage nonlinear 
multi-objective optimization planning model for integrating Distributed Energy Resources (DERs), including 
wind Distributed Generations (DGs), photovoltaic (PV) DGs, stationary Battery Energy Storage Systems (SBESSs), 
and mobile Battery Energy Storage Systems (MBESSs), over a 10-year project horizon. The model evaluates the 
efficiency and cost-effectiveness of hybrid SBESS-MBESS systems to enhance Renewable Energy Source (RES) 
integration within the electric power distribution system (DS) while addressing technical, environmental, and 
economic objectives. It minimizes total expected planning, operation, and emission costs, power loss, and voltage 
deviation by determining the optimal locations and capacities for wind DGs, PV DGs, and SBESSs, and by 
establishing a monthly transportation schedule for MBESSs. The optimization also coordinates the charging and 
discharging profiles of SBESSs and MBESSs to maximize green energy utilization and minimize system costs. 
Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) models uncertainties in wind speed, solar irradiation, load power, and energy 
prices, while the backward reduction method (BRM) mitigates computational complexities. A hybrid optimi -
zation approach combining the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGAII) and multi-objective particle 
swarm optimization (MOPSO) with a decision-making algorithm is proposed to solve the planning problem. 
Simulations on a 69-bus DS demonstrate significant reductions in long-term costs (37.72 %), power loss (41.58 
%), and voltage deviation (47.07 %) achieved by the hybrid SBESS-MBESS system compared to other configu -
rations, underscoring its potential to enhance renewable energy integration and system performance in tran -
sitioning energy systems.

1. Introduction
1.1. Motivation
Global focus on environmental preservation grows due to pollution 
from traditional generators. Priority is shifting towards adopting 
renewable energy sources (RESs) through distributed generations (DGs) 
like wind and solar PV systems. Challenges remain with RESs ’ inter -
mittent nature, requiring precise forecasting and resilient solutions 
[ 1 – 3 ]. Advancements in power electronics drive Energy Storage Systems 
(ESSs) adoption, mitigating RES unpredictability by storing excess en -
ergy and releasing it when needed. However, realizing the full benefits 
of deploying storage devices in a distribution system (DS) necessitates 
strategic decisions on their placement, capacity, and management, 
demanding intelligent programming algorithms for optimal configura -
tion [ 4 – 6 ]. Additionally, the increasing adoption of Mobile Battery En -
ergy Storage Systems (MBESSs) [ 7 ] significantly optimize RES 
integration. MBESSs offer mobility, enabling cost-effective relocation to 
optimize performance amidst changing weather and energy demand. 
Additionally, their rapid deployment to disaster-prone zones boosts 
system resilience [ 8 ].
Moreover, the combination of SBESS and MBESS offers a comple -
mentary approach to addressing the challenges of RES integration by 
combining stability and adaptability. SBESS provides a reliable foun -
dation for consistent energy management in fixed locations, while 
MBESS enhances flexibility through its mobility, enabling rapid relo -
cation to areas with fluctuating demand, intermittent generation, or 
disaster recovery needs. This hybrid approach improves system resil -
ience, ensuring continuity of power supply during disruptions and sta -
bilizing the grid under normal conditions. It also optimizes cost 
efficiency by balancing investment and operational costs, with MBESS 
reducing the need for over-provisioning and SBESS supporting long- 
term energy storage. Together, they maximize renewable energy utili -
zation by addressing spatial and temporal mismatches, with MBESS 
capturing and delivering energy dynamically and SBESS storing surplus 
energy for sustained use. This dual system further allows for tailored 
optimization of location, capacity, and operational profiles, effectively 
tackling technical, economic, and environmental challenges in RES 
integration [ 4 – 7 ], and [ 8 ].
Furthermore, the use of Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) and the 
Backward Reduction Method (BRM) directly supports achieving the 
stated objectives (technical, economic, and environmental) by 
addressing uncertainties inherent in RESs and energy demand. MCS 
models the variability of RESs generation and demand through proba -
bilistic scenarios, while BRM condenses these scenarios into a manage -
able subset, maintaining statistical accuracy and reducing 
computational complexity. This ensures robust optimization of SBESS 
and MBESS placement, capacity, and management under uncertain 
conditions, leading to cost-effective and reliable solutions. Additionally, 
these methods refine MBESS deployment schedules and charging/dis -
charging profiles for both SBESS and MBESS, enhancing energy utili -
zation and minimizing losses. By effectively managing variability, this 
approach maximizes green energy integration, reduces costs and emis -
sions, and strengthens system resilience, aligning with the technical, 
economic, and environmental objectives [ 3 , 9 ].
1.2. Aim and objectives
This paper introduces a comprehensive long-term stochastic mixed- 
integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) multi-objective optimization 
planning model specifically designed to incorporate RESs (wind and PV 
DGs), SBESSs, and MBESSs over a 10-year project duration. The study 
emphasizes addressing uncertainties in critical stochastic variables, such 
as wind speed, solar irradiation, load power, and energy prices, using 
advanced simulation and scenario reduction techniques. The study aims 
to achieve the following objectives. 
• Enhance RESs Integration: Evaluate the efficiency and cost- 
effectiveness of deploying a hybrid blend of SBESS and MBESS to 
maximize the integration of RESs within the electric power DS.
• Minimize Objective Functions: Simultaneously optimize three key 
metrics: 
✓ Total expected planning, operation, and emission costs.
✓ Total Power losses in the DS.
✓ Voltage deviations across the system.
• Optimize System Configuration: Determine the optimal locations and 
capacities for wind DGs, PV DGs, and SBESSs while integrating 
MBESSs for dynamic deployment.
• Develop Transportation Schedules: Establish a monthly trans -
portation schedule for MBESSs to ensure efficient energy distribution 
and system reliability.
• Optimize Energy Profiles: Coordinate charging and discharging 
profiles of both SBESSs and MBESSs to balance energy availability 
and minimize system costs.
• Address System Uncertainties: Use MCS to model stochastic un -
certainties and the BRM to reduce computational complexities.
1.3. Literature review
The integration of RESs into power systems has been a focal point of 
recent research, with ESSs such as SBESSs and MBESSs identified as 
pivotal solutions to address challenges related to variability, cost, and 
system resilience. Below, the literature is categorized into thematic 
subheadings for clarity and relevance.
1.3.1. Optimal planning of SBESSs with RESs
Several studies have explored the optimal planning and operation of 
SBESSs for enhanced integration of RESs into DSs. The studies in Refs. 
[ 10 – 12 ], and [ 13 ] proposed optimization models for the optimal 
placement, capacity, and power rating of SBESSs in DSs and generation 
systems, emphasizing wind power integration. Notably [ 10 ], employed 
the five-point estimation method (5-PEM) to handle wind power un -
certainties, while [ 11 ] extended the approach to DS-level optimization.

Hybrid optimization techniques like NSGAII-MOPSO were applied in 
Ref. [ 10 ] to enhance efficiency. Similarly [ 12 , 13 ], introduced a 
two-stage planning and operation model focusing on optimal com -
pressed air ESS placement and scheduling to minimize total DS costs 
while addressing wind power uncertainties.
From a techno-economic perspective, study [ 14 ] developed a 
short-term planning model to integrate wind DGs, PV DGs, SBESSs, and 
Plug-in Electric Vehicle Parking Lots (PEV-PLs), optimizing both resil -
ience and cost-effectiveness. Similarly, study [ 15 ] evaluated the eco -
nomic feasibility of SBESSs in DSs under various uncertainties, including 
battery degradation and RESs variability. In study [ 16 ], a Modified Salp 
Swarm Algorithm (MSSA) was applied for the techno-economic opti -
mization of SBESS sizing and bi-directional converter integration across 
diverse environmental scenarios.
1.3.2. Optimal planning of MBESSs with RESs
The integration of MBESSs with RESs has garnered increasing 
attention due to their flexibility and mobility. Several studies have 
focused on optimizing the transportation and scheduling of MBESSs to 
enhance the integration of RESs. Studies [ 7 , 17–19 ], and [ 20 ] focused on 
the optimal scheduling and relocation of MBESSs to enhance RES inte -
gration. In Ref. [ 7 ], a MINLP model was developed to optimize the 
deployment of MBESSs in conjunction with wind DGs and PV DGs. Study 
[ 17 ] proposed a novel joint optimization strategy integrating MBESSs 
with wind DGs, PV DGs, and hydropower in DSs. Using a MINLP 
approach with deep reinforcement learning (DRL), the study optimized 
MBESS operations, demonstrating substantial reductions in costs, 
congestion, and improved RES penetration. The authors in Ref. [ 18 ] 
proposed a model to manage MBESSs as mobile charging stations for EVs 
during peak loads, while [ 19 ] developed a MILP framework to minimize 
DS operational costs by optimizing MBESS transportation and charging 
profiles. Study [ 20 ] introduced a multi-stage scheduling problem to 
address day-ahead and real-time optimization of MBESSs, achieving 
superior PV penetration rates and reduced costs. While most studies 
emphasized hourly or daily scheduling [ 7 ], uniquely explored monthly 
scheduling. However, this work lacked integration of SBESSs, focused 
solely on economic objectives, and did not evaluate hybrid 
SBESS-MBESS systems comprehensively.
MBESSs have been integrated into resilience frameworks for DSs and 
Energy Hubs (EHs) to enhance their performance during emergencies. In 
Ref. [ 21 ], stochastic optimization with joint probability constraints was 
applied to restore power in emergencies, while [ 22 ] evaluated MBESS 
deployment in an EH under hurricane scenarios, integrating components 
like hydrogen ESS and combined heat and power units.
1.3.3. Hybrid integration of SBESSs and MBESSs
Few studies have addressed the synergistic benefits of hybrid SBESS- 
MBESS systems. The study in Ref. [ 23 ] examined hybrid SBESS-MBESS 
planning for a one-year project. Results showed that while SBESSs 
enhanced cost-effectiveness and MBESSs improved EV fleet penetration, 
their hybridization offered limited advantages for the considered time -
frame. In Refs. [ 24 , 25 ], hybrid systems were evaluated in 
grid-connected multi-microgrid (MG) setups. The studies highlighted 
the potential of hybrid ESSs to enhance system resilience by leveraging 
SBESS for local stability and MBESS for flexible redistribution during 
normal and contingency scenarios. Additionally [ 24 ], proposed a 
multi-level energy management system (EMS) to optimize the coordi -
nation of SBESS and MBESS for islanded and connected MG operations.

1.3.4. Advanced optimization models for RES-ESS integration
Several works have focused on advanced optimization and uncer -
tainty modeling methodologies for RES-ESS integration. For instance, 
studies [ 27 , 28 ], and [ 29 ] employed hybrid metaheuristic algorithms, 
such as NSGAII-MOPSO, for long-term planning models. These models 
optimized the placement, sizing, and operation of wind DGs, PV DGs, 
SBESSs, and Demand Response Programs (DRPs) in DSs, achieving sig -
nificant cost savings and improved RES integration. Moreover [ 29 ], 
extended the scope to include PEV-PLs, showcasing the added benefits of 
coordinated ESS-DRP systems. Furthermore, the study in Ref. [ 28 ] built 
upon the methodologies presented in Refs. [ 27 , 29 ], and [ 30 ] restruc -
turing them into a two-stage, short-term (one-year) framework. This 
framework optimized the allocation of wind DGs, PV DGs, and SBESSs 
while incorporating time-shifting DRPs and network reconfiguration 
strategies.
From an uncertainty management perspective, studies [ 12 , 31 ] 
modeled uncertainties associated with wind speed, solar irradiation, 
load power, and energy prices using advanced techniques such as the 
five-point estimation method (5-PEM) and Monte Carlo Simulation 
(MCS). These models aimed to minimize planning and operational costs 
while enhancing system reliability. Similarly, study [ 32 ] introduced an 
adaptive resilience planning model that utilized AC Optimal Power Flow 
(AC OPF) to integrate SBESSs and RESs into networked microgrids, 
effectively addressing uncertainties and contingencies.
The studies in Refs. [ 33 , 34 ], and [ 35 ] focused on similar topics. The 
common contributions of these studies focus on optimizing BESS and 
RESs integration into DSs to enhance technical performance (improved 
voltage profiles, reduced line losses, and peak demand management) 
and minimize economic costs (installation, replacement, and operation 
and maintenance). Advanced metaheuristic algorithms like PSO, African 
Vulture Optimization Algorithm (AVOA), Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA), 
and Crayfish Optimization Algorithm (COA) address complex non-linear 
optimization problems, ensuring robust solutions. Fixed Li-ion batteries 
are emphasized for their high efficiency and cost-effectiveness, sup -
porting renewable energy variability and system resilience. These works 
collectively advance efficient, sustainable, and reliable energy systems.
Furthermore, ESSs have been effectively employed in resilience- 
oriented frameworks. For example, studies [ 36 , 37 ], and [ 32 ] proposed 
resilience-focused optimization strategies for MGs. These studies 
emphasized minimizing costs and maximizing system reliability through 
the optimal coordination of RESs, SBESSs, and Plug-in Electric Vehicles 
(PEVs).
1.3.5. Emerging applications of ESSs
Emerging research has broadened the scope of ESSs beyond tradi -
tional DSs to include EHs and Multi-Energy MGs. For instance, studies 
[ 22 , 24 ], and [ 25 ] examined the role of ESSs in networked MGs and EHs, 
emphasizing resilience and energy distribution efficiency. These models 
integrated diverse resources such as hydrogen ESSs, thermal ESSs, and 
combined heat and power units to effectively address multi-energy de -
mands. Moreover, ESSs play a crucial role in supporting Vehicle-to-Grid 
(V2G) integration. For example, studies [ 38 , 39 ], and [ 40 ] leveraged 
Electric Vehicle (EV) batteries as mobile ESSs, contributing to energy 
management and demand-side optimization. Hierarchical frameworks 
and clustering control techniques were utilized to optimize EV sched -
uling and enhance renewable energy utilization. Specifically, study [ 38 ] 
applied Model Predictive Control (MPC) to integrate EV batteries as 
MBESSs in smart homes, optimizing both comfort and energy 
expenditure.
1.4. Research gaps
Drawing upon a thorough examination of the literature presented in 
Table 1 and leveraging the combined expertise of the authors, it is 
evident that previous research efforts have explored the integration of 
MBESS into the DS to varying extents. Notably, prior research works 
[ 7 – 17 ] that incorporated MBESSs primarily focused on either hourly or 
daily transportation schedules. In contrast, this study introduces a dy -
namic approach by employing a monthly transportation schedule for 
MBESSs. This novel strategy offers several advantages over the meth -
odologies utilized in the existing literature [ 17 – 26 ].
From a practical standpoint, using a monthly transportation schedule 
for MBESSs instead of an hourly schedule offers several advantages. 
• Reduced Operational Complexity: Monthly scheduling simplifies 
logistics and minimizes relocations, reducing the need for extensive 
coordination and resources.
• Lower Transportation Costs: Fewer relocations result in reduced 
expenses for fuel, vehicle wear and tear, and manpower.
• Improved Predictability and Planning: Monthly schedules align with 
seasonal and long-term energy planning cycles, ensuring stability 
and practicality.
• Mitigation of Wear and Tear: Less frequent movement reduces 
physical stress on MBESS units, extending their lifespan and lowering 
maintenance costs.
• Adaptation to RES Variability: Monthly scheduling aligns with sea -
sonal variability in RESs, avoiding unnecessary adjustments to 
minor, short-term fluctuations.
However, the study in Ref. [ 7 ] stands as the sole work in the litera -
ture focusing on the monthly transportation scheduling of MBESS to 
enhance RESs penetration. However, several limitations were identified 
within this work. 
• SBESS integration was not addressed.
• Solely economic analysis was conducted, overlooking crucial tech -
nical objectives that could impact system security and associated 
costs.
• The comparison was limited to the basic system versus the system 
with MBESS.
• The hybrid integration of SBESSs and MBESSs and their comparative 
impacts on system planning and operation objectives were not 
investigated.
• A comprehensive and in-depth analysis was lacking.
Furthermore, several research works presented in Table 1 did not 
incorporate a combination of SBESSs and MBESSs. This study addresses 
this gap by leveraging the benefits of such a hybrid integration. The 
advantages of combining SBESSs and MBESSs can be summarized as 
follows. 
• Flexibility in Energy Distribution: SBESSs provide localized, stable 
storage, while MBESSs offer mobility to redistribute energy to high- 
demand areas every month.
• Optimal Resource Utilization: SBESSs operate continuously, while 
MBESSs are relocated strategically to prioritize evolving needs, 
reducing inefficiencies and uncertainties (e.g., the monthly changes 
in weather conditions can significantly affect wind speed, solar 
irradiation, load levels, and energy prices).
• Cost-Effectiveness: The hybrid approach minimizes capital and 
operational expenses by balancing stationary and mobile storage 
capacities effectively.

2. Methodology
2.1. Model framework
Governments are actively encouraging utilities to incorporate 
renewable DG systems, such as wind and PV, as part of efforts to 
decarbonize the power industry. This strategic deployment aims to 
reduce reliance on conventional energy sources, consequently lowering 
operational costs and carbon emissions. However, the intermittent and 
unpredictable nature of such DGs poses challenges, potentially limiting 
their integration levels to avoid compromising system security. Addi -
tionally, their unreliability during and after natural or man-made di -
sasters further underscores these challenges.
To enhance the integration of renewable DGs, ESSs, particularly 
SBESSs, emerge as the optimal solution. SBESSs can store surplus energy 
generated by DGs and dispatch it during shortage periods, thereby 
smoothing out fluctuations. However, before deployment, a compre -
hensive planning strategy must be devised to ensure optimal operation 
and economic viability of all system components. Developing effective 
planning models that account for uncertainties associated with renew -
able DGs and SBESSs is essential for boosting green energy penetration. 
Moreover, introducing MBESSs capable of relocating monthly to adapt 
to variable weather conditions, such as wind speed and solar irradiation, 
presents an additional avenue for enhancing green energy penetration. 
The flexibility of MBESSs to relocate to vulnerable areas post-disaster 
further strengthens system resilience. Although most of the existing 
literature utilized MBESSs for contingency cases, the author ’ s decision to 
include MBESSs as a planning object under normal operating conditions 
reflects their strategic vision for leveraging MBESSs beyond traditional 
emergency use cases. Below are the key reasons and rationale. 
• Flexibility for Intermittency: MBESSs address the variability of RESs 
by relocating to areas with energy imbalances or higher renewable 
generation, based on a monthly schedule.
• Dynamic Resource Allocation: MBESSs dynamically redistribute en -
ergy to critical grid locations, improving RES integration even during 
normal operations.
• Cost Efficiency: Their deployment reduces the need for over- 
investment in SBESSs while maintaining operational flexibility.
• Economic Optimization: MBESSs contribute to significant cost re -
ductions, including planning, operation, and emissions, over a 10- 
year horizon.

2.2. Uncertainty modelling
In this section, MCS presented in Ref. [ 3 ] is utilized to generate 1000 
independent scenarios, incorporating probability density functions 
(PDFs) of multiple input stochastic variables, including wind speed, 
solar irradiation, load power, and energy prices. However, the extensive 
sample size (S) may result in significant computational demands. To 
mitigate this challenge, the BRM is employed. This method efficiently 
reduces the S to 2 scenarios per month, each associated with its 
respective probabilities while maintaining acceptable accuracy in pre -
dicting the actual output variables.
Despite reducing the number of scenarios, BRM ensures that the 
reduced set still captures the key statistical characteristics of the original 
uncertainty distribution. This means that the reduced set of scenarios is 
likely to provide a close approximation to the actual outcomes without a 
significant loss in accuracy. The overall expected values and variances of 
the stochastic variables remain representative, even with fewer sce -
narios. For example, consider a scenario where the system needs to ac -
count for a range of energy prices that could vary dramatically over 
time. Instead of evaluating all possible energy price scenarios (which 
might result in hundreds or thousands of distinct scenarios), BRM can 
select just a few representative scenarios — say, two per month. These 
selected scenarios might capture the major fluctuations in energy prices 
without requiring the model to process every potential variation. This 
drastically cuts down on computational time while still ensuring that the 
model can handle the major fluctuations in energy prices effectively. A 
detailed procedural outline of MCS can be found in our prior publication 
[ 31 ] while the steps for applying the BRM are elaborated in Refs. [ 41 ,
42 ]. These procedures are succinctly summarized in the proposed 
framework depicted in Fig. 1 . Furthermore, the selected PDFs for the 
uncertain variables are presented in Appendix A to maintain readability.
2.3. Problem formulation
This section outlines the objective functions of the proposed plan -
ning model. It details the technical constraints applied to the compo -
nents of the DS, encompassing wind DG, PV DG, SBESS, MBESS, DS 
substation (DSS), feeders, and buses. Additionally, it introduces the 
devised charging and discharging control strategy for the assigned 
SBESSs and MEBSSs. It should be noted that the optimization problem is 
formulated as a MINLP model because the optimization problem in -
volves complex relationships, including non-linear objective functions 
(e.g., energy costs, emissions, and power losses), and the need to model 
both continuous variables (e.g., capacities, energy storage levels) and 
discrete decision variables (e.g., the locations and operational statuses of 
distributed energy resources like DGs and BESSs). The MINLP formula -
tion allows for the inclusion of these non-linearities and discrete de -
cisions simultaneously, making it well-suited to address the system ’ s 
complexity in integrating RESs, storage systems, and optimizing system 
operations.

3. Optimization solution method
The employed solving methodology comprises a hybrid 
probabilistic-optimization-decision-making algorithm amalgamating 
NSGAII-MOPSO-MCS-BRM-PLF-TOPSIS. This amalgamation is designed 
to address the planning model delineated in preceding sections. The PSO 
algorithm, noted for its simplicity, speed, and robustness, serves as the 
foundational method. Consequently, a multi-objective variant, MOPSO, 
is introduced to tackle the optimization conundrum. Conversely, NSGAII 
boasts the advantage of fostering a richer diversity of solutions through 
the crowding comparison operator while upholding superior solutions 
via elitism. Thus, the fusion of NSGAII and MOPSO promises an 
enhanced exploration of the search space, culminating in the attainment 
of optimal global solutions [ 44 ]. Detailed guidelines for the effective 
implementation of the adopted hybrid algorithm in resolving the MINLP 
issue and achieving optimal solutions by minimizing the aforemen -
tioned objective functions are extensively elucidated in our antecedent 
research endeavors [ 10 – 12 , 31 , 45 ].

4. Results and discussions
To assess the efficacy of the proposed planning model in determining 
the optimal number, placement, capacity, and hourly scheduling pro -
jections for a diverse array of DERs, encompassing wind DGs, PV DGs, 
SBESSs, and MBESSs, while concurrently minimizing three explicitly 
defined long term objective functions aimed at optimizing the integra -
tion of RESs, the 69-bus DS [ 7 ] has been selected as the focal point for 
this case study, as illustrated in Fig. 4 .
The proposed planning model was implemented in MATLAB 
(R2023b) on a personal laptop equipped with 12 GB of RAM and an Intel 
Core i7-5500U processor operating at a clock speed of 2.56 GHz. 
Experimental simulations encompassed 24-h simulations considering 
the number of the reduced scenarios, spanning 12 months over a 10-year 
planning horizon, considering annual load growth. The computational 
time for each case was notably extensive, taking nearly two days to 
complete. Consequently, applying the entire methodology on MATLAB 
for a single system, such as a 69-bus DS, required approximately one 
week to extract all results for all four cases. Extending this methodology 
to multiple systems, particularly larger ones with significantly more 
variables and uncertainties, would likely demand more than one week 
per system. This considerable computational burden makes testing on 
multiple systems impractical and time-consuming. As a result, this study 
focused on demonstrating the methodology on a single system (69-bus 
DS).

5. Conclusions
This paper presents a long-term optimization model integrating 
DERs like wind DGs, PV DGs, SBESSs, and MBESSs over 10 years. It aims 
to assess the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of a hybrid SBESS-MBESS 
deployment for RES integration, addressing multiple objective func -
tions. The model minimizes total planning, operation, and emission 
costs, power loss, and voltage deviation. It determines optimal locations 
and capacities for DERs, establishes a monthly MBESS transportation 
schedule, and optimizes charging profiles. Monte Carlo Simulation and 
backward reduction method handle system uncertainty efficiently. The 
outcomes of this work are summarized as follows. 
• Optimally deploying SBESS alone, MBESS alone, or hybrid SBESS- 
MBESS results in the same RESs capacity of 3.65MVA.
• Optimal deployment scenarios yield 10 SBESSs with a total capacity 
of (3.69 MWh, 0.738MVA), or 10 MBESSs with a total capacity of 
(3.6 MWh, 0.72MVA), or 4 SBESSs and 4 MBESSs with a much lower 
total capacity of (2.25 MWh, 0.45MVA) when utilizing SBESS alone 
or MBESS alone or hybrid SBESS-MBESS.
• Deploying Wind/PV/MBESS optimally reduces DSS total operation 
and emission costs by 55.46 %, 0.021 %, and 3.67 % compared to the 
base case, SBESS alone with wind and PV DGs, and hybrid SBESSs- 
MBESSs with wind and PV DGs, respectively.
• Optimally deploying hybrid SBESS-MBESS with wind and PV DGs 
reduces total investment, operation, and transportation costs of 
BESSs by 65.81 % and 71.45 % compared to the case of utilizing 
SBESS alone or MBESS alone.
• Substantial reductions in total investment, operation, and trans -
portation costs of employed BESSs result in a total reduction of 37.72 
%, 0.16 %, and 0.62 % in long-term expected costs compared to the 
base case, SBESS alone, and MBESS alone.
• Optimal deployment of hybrid SBESSs-MBESSs with wind DGs and 
PV DGs reduces total expected power loss by 41.58 %, 6.27 %, and 
6.73 %, and total expected voltage deviation by 47.07 %, 3.83 %, and 
6.14 %, compared to the base case, SBESS alone with wind and PV 
DGs, and MBESS alone with wind and PV DGs.
In summary, integrating MBESS and SBESS offers superior results by 
leveraging their complementary features: MBESS provides mobility and 
flexibility for dynamic needs, while SBESS ensures stability and cost- 
effective baseline support. Key advantages include dynamic deploy -
ment of MBESS to critical locations for voltage regulation, consistent 
long-term support from SBESS, optimized energy distribution, enhanced 
renewable energy integration, reduced power losses, improved voltage 
profiles, and adaptability to uncertainties in demand and generation. 
However, limitations such as transportation challenges for MBESS and 
the computational complexity of hybrid system optimization must be 
addressed for broader practical application. Future research could focus
